translations.text: There shall be signs in the sun and moon and stars: and so on.
The evangelist Luke wrote in today's gospel that our Lord spoke these words to his disciples about the signs that will happen before the end of this world.
The Lord said, "There shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars, and on earth there shall be distress of nations," and so on.

The holy Gregory explained the hidden meaning of this gospel to us, beginning like this: The Lord our Redeemer wishes to find us ready, and so he made known the evils that follow the ageing world, so that he might hold us back from loving it.
He showed how many sufferings come before the ending of this world, so that if we will not fear God in tranquility, we may at least fear his approaching judgment, terrified by various afflictions.
Earlier in this reading the Saviour said, "Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom, and there shall be great earthquakes everywhere, and plague, and famine."

And then, among these things, he said this: "There shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars, and on earth distress of nations, because of the turmoil and roaring of the sea's waves."
Some of these signs we have seen fulfilled; others we fear are still to come.
Truly, in these recent days nations have risen against nations, and their distress on earth has been worse than what we read of in old books.
Earthquakes have often overthrown many cities in various places, as happened in the days of the emperor Tiberius, when thirteen cities fell in an earthquake.
We are often afflicted with plague and famine, but we have not yet seen any clear signs in the sun, or in the moon, or in the stars.

We read in astronomy that the sun is sometimes darkened when the moon's disc passes in front of it, and also that the full moon suddenly changes colour when it is cut off from the sun's light by the earth's shadow.
There are also some stars with beams of light, which suddenly rise and quickly depart, and their rising always signals something new:
but the Lord did not mean these signs in the gospel prophecy. He meant the terrible signs that will come before the great day.
Matthew the evangelist wrote of these signs more clearly, saying, "Immediately after the great tribulation the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall give no light,
and stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven shall be shaken, and then the sign of Christ's cross shall appear in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn."

The turmoil of the sea and the roaring of the waves have not yet broken out in an unusual way. But since many of the signs mentioned above have been fulfilled, there is no doubt that the few that remain will certainly be fulfilled.
My brothers, these things are written so that our minds may stay watchful and on guard, so that they do not grow slack through feeling secure, nor grow sick through ignorance;
but so that the fear may always keep them occupied, and their watchfulness may strengthen them in good works.
The Lord said, "Men shall wither away for fear and expectation of the things that shall come upon the whole world.
Truly the powers of heaven shall be shaken." The powers of heaven are angels and archangels, thrones, principalities, dominions and powers.
These hosts of angels shall be shown visibly to our sight at the coming of the strict Judge, so that they may sternly exact from us what the invisible Creator now patiently bears with.
Then we shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and majesty.

The Lord called himself the Son of Man more often than the Son of God, because of the humility of the human nature he had taken on, so that he might remind us of the nature that he took on for our sake.
He is truly the Son of man, and not the Son of men, and there is no other son of one human being except Christ alone.

He shall be revealed in power and majesty to those who would not listen to him while he dwelt in humility, so that they may then feel his might all the more severely, just as much as they now refuse to bow their necks to his patience.
These words are spoken about the reprobate, but here follow the words that comfort the elect.
The Saviour said, "When these wonders begin, then lift up your heads and look, because your redemption is drawing near."
It is as if he plainly urged his elect: 'When the world's torments increase, when the terror of the great judgement is revealed, then lift up your heads,
that is, rejoice in your minds, because when this world, which you did not love, is ended, then the redemption that you sought is at hand.'
In holy scripture the head is often put for a person's mind, because the head guides the other limbs, just as the mind directs the thoughts.
We lift up our heads when we raise our minds to the joy of the heavenly homeland.
Those who love God are exhorted to rejoice at the ending of the world, because when the world, which they did not love, passes away, then truly they will find him whom they loved.
God forbid that any believer who desires to see God should mourn for the downfall of the world;
it is truly written, "Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be counted as God's enemy."
Truly, whoever does not rejoice as the end of the world draws near shows that he was its friend, and he is then convicted of being God's enemy.
But let friendship with this world depart from the hearts of believing people, and let it depart from those who believe that the other life is to come and who love it through their deeds.
It is those who have planted the roots of their heart in love of the world who must mourn for its destruction, those who do not seek the life to come, nor even believe in it:
we, who have truly come to know the joy of the heavenly homeland in full, must hasten towards it with one mind.
We ought to know that we should travel there quickly and arrive by the shorter way, because this world is afflicted with many sorrows and troubled by perversities.
What is this mortal life but a way? Understand now what it is to grow weary from the toil of the way, and yet not want to come to the end of the way.
The Lord said, "Look at the fig tree and all the other trees: when they sprout, then you know that summer is coming.
So also you may know, when you see these foretold signs, that the kingdom of God is drawing near." Truly these words show that the fruit of this world is ruin.
It grows only so that it may fall; it sprouts only so that it may destroy with plagues whatever it sprouted before.
This world is like a man growing old: in youth the body thrives, with a strong chest and full, healthy limbs;
Truly, in old age a man's body is bent, his neck sags, his face is wrinkled, and all his limbs are weakened;
his chest is troubled with sighing, and his breath fails him between words. Even though no illness has hold of him, very often his health is itself a sickness to him.
So it is with this world: at the beginning it was flourishing as if in youth; it was growing in bodily health, and fat with an abundance of riches, long in life, quiet in long-lasting peace;
But now he is overcome by age, as if driven toward death by frequent afflictions.
My brothers, do not love this world, which you see cannot last long.
Concerning this the apostle said, "Do not love the world, nor the things that are in it, because whoever loves the world does not have the love of God in him."
God's kingdom is rightly compared to summertime, because then the mists of our sorrow pass away, and the days of life shine through the brightness of the eternal sun.
All the things said above are confirmed with great certainty by the saying that follows: "Truly I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things come to pass."
The Lord spoke these words to the Jewish nation, and their race will not pass away through decay before this world comes to an end.
With this meaning the apostle Paul said that "the Lord himself will come down from heaven at the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet of God, and the dead will rise first;
then we who are living and are found in the body will be caught up together with the others in the clouds to meet Christ, and so we will be with God forever after."
Comfort yourselves with these words." The Evangelist Matthew also agrees with this meaning, in these words,
"The Lord will send his angels with trumpets and a great voice, and they will gather his chosen ones from the four winds, from all the ends of the earth up to the high heavens."
The apostle said, "We who are living." By those words he did not mean himself, but those who remain alive until the end of this world.
This also shows that mankind will not perish entirely before the end. Yet those who are found alive at that time will still undergo a brief death;
for a heavenly fire will sweep over the whole world in a single burning, and the dead will rise from their graves along with the fire,
and the living will be killed by the heat of the fire and at once brought back to life for eternal things.
The fire will do no harm at all to the righteous, who were cleansed from sins beforehand; but whoever is not cleansed will feel the blast of the fire. And then we will all come to the Judgement.
The judgment will not be held on any earthly field, but it will be as the apostle said above in this reading: that we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ, through this air;

and there will be the separation of righteous men and wicked. Afterwards the righteous will dwell nowhere except with God in the kingdom of heaven, and the wicked nowhere except with the devil in the torments of hell.
The Saviour ended this gospel with these words: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away."

Heaven and earth will not turn into nothing. Instead, they will be changed from the form they now have into a better form, as John the Evangelist said: "Then there will be a new heaven and a new earth."
Indeed, no others will be created; these will be renewed.
Heaven and earth will pass away, and yet they will endure, because they will be cleansed by fire from the form that they now have, and nevertheless they will always remain in their own nature.
Then the sun will be seven times brighter than it is now, and the moon will have the light of the sun.
David truly prophesied about Christ's coming in these words: "God will come openly, and he will not keep silent.
Fire burns in his sight, and around him there is a violent storm." The storm washes away whatever the fire burns up.
About that day the prophet Zephaniah said, "The great day of God is very near, and exceedingly swift: bitter will be the voice of that day; there the strong man will be troubled.
That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and anguish, a day of misery and lamentation, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of the trumpet and of outcry."
My brothers, set the remembrance of this day before your eyes, and whatever now seems burdensome will all be made light in comparison with it.
Correct your lives and change your ways; punish your evil deeds with weeping; resist the temptations of the devil;
turn away from evil and do good, and you will be as much more free of care at the coming of the eternal Judge as you now forestall his severity with fear.
The prophet said that the great day of God is very near and exceedingly swift. Even if there were still another thousand years until that day, it would not be long;
for whatever comes to an end is short and quick, and once it has ended, it is as if it had never happened.

And even if it were a long time until that day, which it is not, our own time is still not long, and at our end it will be judged for us whether we must await the general judgment in rest or in torment.
Let us therefore use the time that God has given us, and earn eternal life with him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.
